vignette:
Daniel Voss had been working the closing shift at a small grocery-and-home goods store when the disaster began, one of those chaotic, man-made incidents that made no sense even as it was happening. A man came in shouting about a dispute outside and threw a heavy object through the front entrance, sending people scattering and knocking over a display near the register. Daniel remembered the scene not as a continuous story but as a handful of brutal stills: the glass exploding across the tile, a woman crouching with her hands over her head, the hard press of another customer's shoulder jammed against him in the rush to get away. Even now, the memory arrived with an awful clarity that felt more real than the everyday moments around him, as if those images had been burned into him while ordinary life had stayed faint and less substantial. What he hated most was the shame that came with remembering it. He had been embarrassed by how frozen he felt, by how he had failed to help more decisively, and that shame made him recoil from the memory as if it proved something ugly about him.

In the weeks after, Daniel found that certain things at work could pull him back into that night with almost no warning. If a customer stood too close at the checkout lane, leaning over the counter while he bagged items, his body tensed before his mind caught up, because the memory of being trapped in that crush of people came back through his skin. If someone behaved badly in the store - shouting at a cashier, demanding special treatment, cutting in line with a sneer - he felt a surge of anger and alarm that seemed bigger than the moment, because disorder and selfishness now carried the flavor of the disaster for him. Even the feel of a particular rough, gritty texture could jolt him: the kind of coarse material on a torn box corner or an abrasive cleaning pad would make him think, with no logic he trusted, of the debris and broken surfaces from that day. Those moments did not stay contained. They brought the whole scene rushing back in vivid fragments, and the sharper the recollection became, the more intensely he noticed the world for threats that resembled it. Daniel started scanning people's distance from him, watching hands, shoulders, and tone, as if the next bad thing might announce itself through some small physical closeness or another person's bad behavior.

To keep himself from being flooded, he tried hard not to think about it at all. When an image of the shattered entrance or the frightened woman flashed up, he would tell himself it had not really happened or that it had not been that bad, as if minimizing it could press the memory flat. But the more he pushed, the more the pictures returned on their own, and the more vivid they became, the more he felt he needed those same defenses again. Sometimes, after a day that had left him pinned by the memory, he would hurt himself physically just enough to interrupt the spiraling thoughts - a sharp, private pain that felt easier to bear than the shame and terror of what he could see in his mind. He came to rely on those moments of distraction when the images got too real, yet they left him more on edge afterward, more primed to notice every close-pressed stranger in the aisle and every rude customer at the counter as if they were warnings that another catastrophe was about to start. The strategies gave him momentary relief, but they also kept the event alive, bringing it back in harsher detail and tying his attention even tighter to the same triggers.

Over time, Daniel's world narrowed around that cycle. He found himself choosing the end of the aisle with the most room, stepping back from customers, and making sure he had an escape route whenever the store got crowded. When someone brushed past him in a tight space, the memory would hit with full force; when the memory hit, he would clamp down harder, try not to think, or resort to hurting himself to break the loop. That only made the images return sharper, and with them came a need to watch for the next proximity, the next sign of misbehavior, the next coarse texture that might set it all off again. At home, his wife noticed how little he said about work and how quickly he changed the subject when she asked about the store. He had begun telling himself, especially on bad nights, that the whole incident was exaggerated or somehow unreal, but the very need to say that made it feel less convincing to him. Recently he finally sought help after a crowded afternoon shift left him shaking in the stockroom, ashamed by how close he had come to hurting himself again just to stop the images. He was coming in hoping to find a way to make the memories feel less like present-tense emergencies, and fearing that if they stayed this vivid much longer, he would keep retreating from work, from his wife, and from the life that still felt precariously close to the disaster.
